reflection_text.6:
The deliberation is centred on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA – a written electronic-monitoring policy for 25+ employers in force 1 Jan 2022 and a written disconnecting-from-work policy for 25+ employers in force 2 June 2022, with a requirement to give the policy to employees on hire and to give an updated copy within 30 days of a change. Threshold is the big split.

A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023, 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023. Unanimously <25 on the date in issue, so no statutory disconnect/electronic-monitoring duty. Compliant in not having a policy.

B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. Below 25 so no statutory disconnect/electronic-monitoring duty is triggered. Voluntary policies exist since 2020/2021. The refusal to give those voluntary policies to new hires on cost grounds is argued by some colleagues as a statutory distribution breach – e.g., Colleague 12, 18, 2, 4 – on the basis of a 10+ disconnect expansion or that electronic monitoring must be distributed whenever monitoring occurs. The majority view is that with <25 employees the policy duties are not engaged and refusing to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach.

C: ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range. Clearly a 25+ employer on both 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022, so both policies are required and the facts say they are written and appropriately distributed. The live disagreement is the monthly update/quarterly hand-out. Colleagues 1, 15, 17, 7 argue this breaches the 30-day update-distribution rule – updating every month but only circulating every fiscal quarter means employees can be >30 days, up to ~90 days, out of date. Colleagues 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 treat the initial “appropriately distributed” statement as sufficient and do not treat the update cadence as decisive on these facts.

D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter, no further change. It has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but no electronic-monitoring policy at all. The core dispute is lock-in vs current headcount. Colleagues 10, 11, 13, 14, 16, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 hold that the 25+ test is met on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and that the obligation crystallises then; the subsequent fall to 24 does not retroactively extinguish the duty that attached on 1 Jan 2022, so the absence of an electronic-monitoring policy by 2 Jan 2023 is a breach. Colleagues 1, 17 treat the obligation as current-headcount based, which would make D <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and therefore not presently required to maintain electronic monitoring.

E: 22 employees on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements, 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023, <25. No statutory disconnect/electronic-monitoring duty on the date in issue. The absence of a disconnect policy is therefore compliant on a 25+ reading.

The 10+ disconnect expansion argued by Colleague 12 would make A, B and E non-compliant for lacking/distributing a disconnect policy and would re-characterise B’s refusal to distribute as a statutory breach. That reading is a minority view in the round.

On balance the most consistently supported statutory breach on a 25+ threshold reading is D’s failure to have a required electronic-monitoring policy that attached on the 30-employee 1 Jan 2022 snapshot, still missing on 2 Jan 2023. C’s monthly-update/quarterly-distribution point is plausible but is the minority position in the current round and the fact pattern explicitly states the policies are “appropriately distributed”. I am retaining the C update-distribution issue and the B distribution/10+ debate as unresolved tensions for later rounds.
reflection_text.17:
The discussion is centred on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments that are in force on 2 Jan 2023: a written electronic-monitoring policy for employers who employ 25 or more employees in Ontario, required for the 25+ cohort as at 1 Jan 2022, and a written disconnecting-from-work policy for employers who employ 25 or more employees, required for the 25+ cohort as at 1 July 2022 / 2 June 2022. The policy must be given to an employee within 30 days of hire and a revised policy must be made available when the policy changes.

A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and through 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023. The eight agreements do not start until 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the material date, no statutory electronic-monitoring / disconnecting obligation is triggered on 2 Jan 2023.

B. 23 employees on the date in issue. <25, so neither the electronic-monitoring nor the disconnecting-from-work policy duties are statutorily engaged. The employer has voluntarily maintained both policies since 2020/2021. Refusal to distribute a voluntary policy to new hires on cost grounds is not a statutory breach on a strict 25+ threshold reading. Colleagues 12,18,4,2 argue the distribution duty would attach once a policy is maintained; the majority view is that no duty attaches because the 25-employee threshold is not met.

C. c.1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Unequivocally >25 on both the 1 Jan 2022 electronic-monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger. The employer states it has written and “appropriately distributed” both policies. The compliance defect raised is the maintenance/distribution of changes: policies are updated every month but a copy is only provided to each employee every fiscal quarter. That can leave employees receiving an updated policy >30 days, often ~90 days, after a change. Colleagues 1,7,15,17 identify this as a breach of the 30-day update / provision obligation for both policies. Colleagues who accept C as compliant read “appropriately distributed” as satisfying the ESA and treat monthly review/quarterly circulation as sufficient practice.

D. 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 24 employees after the 6 terminations on 15 Mar 2022 and no further change. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy and has never developed an electronic-monitoring policy. The split is over threshold assessment. One line, colleagues 10,11,13,14,16, argues the 25-employee test for electronic monitoring crystallises on 1 Jan 2022. Employer D was 30 on that date, so the electronic-monitoring duty attached by 1 Jan 2022 and remains unremedied on 2 Jan 2023, even though current headcount is 24. On that lock-in reading the disconnect obligation is also locked to the 1 Jan 2022 / 1 July 2022 snapshot, and D’s disconnect policy is therefore sufficient, the missing electronic-monitoring policy is the breach. The other line, colleagues 1,7,17, argues the obligation is assessed on current headcount on 2 Jan 2023; 24 employees <25, so no electronic-monitoring / disconnecting duty is presently required and D is compliant on the current-headcount view.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 after August 2022 resignations, 18 after the 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 6 hires are effective 15 Feb 2023, taking headcount to 24. <25 on all relevant dates, no statutory policy duty is triggered as of 2 Jan 2023.

Unresolved issues: the exact effective dates quoted vary – 1 Jan 2022 / 1 July 2022 / 2 June 2022 for disconnect – and whether the 25-employee test is a one-time snapshot on 1 Jan 2022 for the first compliance year or an ongoing current-headcount test. Related to that is whether a drop below 25 after the trigger removes the ongoing maintenance obligation. A further disputed point is the timing of provision of a revised policy: 30 days after a change vs “as soon as practicable”, which drives the C monthly-update / quarterly-distribution analysis. Colleague 12/18’s 10+ employee disconnect expansion as of 1 Jan 2023 would make A and E also non-compliant, and would make B’s refusal to distribute relevant, but that expansion is not established for 2 Jan 2023 under the 2021 Act.

Current leaning: on the prevailing lock-in reading used by the majority of colleagues, D is the employer that is not in compliance as of 2 Jan 2023 for failure to have the electronic-monitoring policy that was triggered by its 30-employee headcount on 1 Jan 2022. The alternative, analytically coherent, reading is that D is compliant on current headcount and C is the breach for failing to provide updated disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies within 30 days of change.
reflection_text.4:
The round-0 pool is split essentially D vs C, with a minority B, and the split turns on three threshold/timing issues.

* Threshold for disconnecting-from-work / electronic monitoring and the date the duty attaches. Most colleagues treat the Working for Workers Act, 2021 duties as 25+ employee duties that crystallise on the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot and, for disconnect, on the 1 July/2 June 2022 effective date. Under that reading:
  - A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 hires do not start until 10 Jan 2023, so 20 <25 on the date in issue. No disconnect / electronic monitoring duty.
  - B: 23 employees on the date in issue, <25, so no statutory disconnect / electronic monitoring duty. Having voluntary policies does not create a statutory distribution obligation; refusal to give a voluntary policy to new hires is not a statutory breach on the 25+ test.
  - E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023, 24 only after the 15 Feb 2023 hires. <25 on all relevant dates. No statutory duty as of 2 Jan 2023.
  - D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, so the 25+ class is met on the transitional lock-in date. Headcount falls to 24 after the 15 Mar 2022 terminations and stays there. The employer has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy but has never developed an electronic monitoring policy. On a lock-in reading the electronic monitoring duty that was triggered by the 1 Jan 2022 30-employee count persists and the absence of a written electronic monitoring policy on 2 Jan 2023 is a breach.

* Current-headcount / post-drop views. Colleagues 1,7,10,17 argue the 25-employee test is ongoing. On that view D after 15 Mar 2022 is a 24-employee employer on 2 Jan 2023, so no current electronic monitoring / disconnect duty, and the disconnect policy it holds is superfluous. That would move the breach elsewhere.

* Update-distribution timing for C. C is unequivocally 25+ throughout 2022, ≈1,000 employees, and states it has written and initially distributed both a disconnecting-from-work and an electronic/online monitoring policy. The contested point is the maintenance/distribution requirement. The ESA requires an updated policy to be provided within 30 days of a change. Updating the policies every month but only issuing a copy to each employee every fiscal quarter means an employee can be working under a policy up to ~90 days out of date. Colleagues 1,15,17 see that as a breach of the 30-day update/distribution obligation for both policies. Colleagues 10,7,16 treat monthly review with quarterly hand-out as ordinary compliance.

* The 10-employee disconnect expansion. Colleagues 12,4,18 note the Working for Workers Act,2022 expansion of the right-to-disconnect duty to 10+ employees effective 1 Jan 2023, with a grace to 2 June 2023 for 10-24 employers. If the 10+ threshold is applied without a grace period, A, B and E would all be within the disconnect class on 2 Jan 2023 and A/E would be in breach for having no policy at all, and B would be in breach for refusing to distribute a policy it voluntarily maintains. That would produce multiple breaches and is inconsistent with the single-answer format.

Unresolved points that remain important for final convergence:
- Exact in-force date of the electronic monitoring duty and whether the duty is assessed on 1 Jan 2022 headcount or on the effective date headcount; colleagues cite 1 Jan 2022, 1 July 2022 and 11 Oct 2022.
- Whether the 25+ obligation, once triggered on 1 Jan 2022, continues after a subsequent drop below 25, or whether the obligation is current-headcount based.
- Whether the disconnect duty for 10-24 employers is immediately operative on 1 Jan 2023 or subject to a 2 June 2023 implementation window.
- Whether C’s monthly update / quarterly distribution practice is a material breach of the 30-day update requirement or an acceptable operational practice.

On the majority lock-in 25+ reading used by most D-voters, D is the clear statutory non-compliance: a 30-employee employer on 1 Jan 2022 that still lacks the required written electronic monitoring policy as of 2 Jan 2023, while the other options are either below threshold on the material dates or have the required policies in place. The C update-distribution issue is the strongest alternative candidate if the obligation is read as current-headcount and the electronic monitoring duty is read as effective only while 25+ is maintained.
reflection_text.11:
The discussion is centred on the Working for Workers Act, 2021 amendments to the ESA and the size thresholds that were in play on 2 Jan 2023.

* Electronic monitoring – 25+ employees.

C

Ontario as at 2 January 2023

* s.74.2 ESA – electronic monitoring: an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario must have a written electronic monitoring policy, give a copy of the policy to each employee within 30 days of hire and give an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. The requirement was in force 1 January 2022 for the 25+ cohort.
* s.74.1 ESA – disconnecting from work: an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario must have a written disconnecting-from-work policy, give a copy to each employee within 30 days of hire and give an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. The requirement was in force for the 25+ cohort 1 July 2022. The 10+ expansion is phased and does not create an immediate policy obligation for the 10-24 cohort on 2 January 2023.

C regularly employs c.1,000 employees in 2022, 987-1,012 at all times, so the 25+ class is met on both the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring trigger date and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger date. The employer has a written electronic monitoring policy and a written disconnecting-from-work policy and the policies have been initially distributed.

The statutory maintenance/distribution duty is not satisfied by merely having a policy in place. Where the policy is changed the employer must provide an updated copy to each employee within 30 days of the change. C amends both the disconnecting-from-work policy and the electronic monitoring policy every month but only hands an updated copy to the workforce once per fiscal quarter. A monthly amendment followed by a quarterly hand-out can leave employees working for up to ~90 days under a superseded version of the policy. That is provision of an updated policy more than 30 days after the change and is a breach of the policy-maintenance/distribution obligation under ss.74.1 and 74.2 ESA for both the disconnecting-from-work and the electronic monitoring regimes.

A is 20 employees on 2 January 2023, the 8 new agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023, so the 25+ electronic monitoring/disconnect duties are not engaged on the date in issue.

B is 23 employees on the date in issue. The 25+ statutory policy duties are not engaged. The employer may voluntarily maintain policies; the ESA does not impose a statutory distribution duty on an employer who is below the 25-employee threshold for a voluntarily adopted policy.

D employed 30 on 1 January 2022 but after the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 headcount is 24 and remains 24 through 2 January 2023. The “regularly employs 25 or more” test is a continuing test. On a current headcount reading D is no longer a 25+ employer on 2 January 2023 and is not statutorily required to maintain an electronic monitoring policy going forward. It does have a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy.

E is 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements, with the 6 hires not effective until 15 February 2023. On 2 January 2023 E employs 18 <25 and is not within the 25+ statutory class for either regime on the date in issue.

On the facts as stated the unambiguous breach on 2 January 2023 is the failure to time the update/distribution of the required policies within 30 days of a change in C.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in play on 2 Jan 2023 are

* s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring – written policy for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario, in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 25+ cohort, policy to be given on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change;
* s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work – written policy for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario, in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort, same give-on-hire and 30-day update/distribution duties.

Headcounts on 2 Jan 2023

* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on date in issue.
* B: 23 on date in issue. <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Voluntary disconnect 2020 and online monitoring 2021.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 30-6 = 24 after 15 Mar 2022 terminations, no further change. 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy; no electronic monitoring policy.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 on 2 Jan 2023, 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. <25 on all relevant dates.
* C: c.1,000 on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. >>25. Written disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring policies, stated as “appropriately distributed”. Policies are updated every month but a copy of the updated policies is provided to each employee only every fiscal quarter.

Core disagreement in round 1

* Snapshot/lock-in reading for D. D was 30 on 1 Jan 2022, so electronic monitoring duty crystallised on 1 Jan 2022 and disconnect duty on the 1 Jan 2022/1 July 2022 qualifying date. Because the duty attached on the qualifying snapshot it persists even though headcount fell to 24 on 15 Mar 2022. Under that reading D has a disconnect policy but no electronic monitoring policy at all on 2 Jan 2023, a categorical breach of s.74.2. This is the majority D position in the current round.
* Ongoing “regularly employs 25+” reading. The 25-employee test is a continuing test assessed on the date in issue. A, B, D and E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 so the 25+ statutory policy duties are not engaged for them on that date. D’s existing disconnect policy is voluntary; absence of an electronic monitoring policy is not required at current headcount. Under this reading the only 25+ employer is C.
  The 30-day update/distribution hook then makes C the breach: C amends both required policies every month but only hands updated copies quarterly, so employees can receive a policy up to ~90 days after a change, i.e. outside the 30-day window required by ss.74.1 and 74.2 for both the disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring regimes. This is the current-headcount C position.

Unresolved/ contested points

* Whether the 25-employee test is a one-time transitional snapshot on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and 1 July 2022 for disconnect, with coverage locked in despite a later fall below 25, or whether “regularly employs 25 or more” is a continuing test assessed on 2 Jan 2023. D is the test case for that.
* Whether C’s “appropriately distributed” description and a quarterly circulation cycle satisfies the 30-day update rule when amendments occur monthly. Some colleagues read monthly updates as routine housekeeping not triggering distribution; others read any monthly change as a material change requiring distribution within 30 days.
* 10+ disconnect expansion. A minority raised a 10-employee disconnect threshold effective 1 Jan 2023 with a compliance window to 2 June 2023. If applied, A and E would also lack a required disconnect policy and B’s refusal to distribute would become a statutory distribution breach, making the question under-determined. The majority round-1 treatment treats the policy duties as 25+ only on 2 Jan 2023.
* Errors noted: electronic monitoring is size-based 25+, not a universal disclosure duty; refusal to distribute a voluntarily adopted policy for an under-threshold employer is not a statutory ESA breach.

Current synthesis retained from prior round and still defensible: under an ongoing regularly employs 25+ reading the statutory policy duties attach only to C on 2 Jan 2023, and C’s monthly amendment/quarterly hand-out practice is a timely-update/distribution breach of the 30-day update requirement for both required policies. D is non-compliant only under a strict 1 Jan 2022 lock-in reading. The snapshot vs ongoing interpretation of the 25-employee test remains the central tension.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D

On 2 January 2023 the two Working for Workers Act, 2021 duties in issue for a 25+ employer are s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring, in force 1 January 2022, and s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work, in force 2 June / 1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort. Both require a written policy to be given to an employee within 30 days of hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy.

The transitional coverage for the initial rollout is fixed by the 1 January 2022 headcount. An employer who employed 25 or more employees in Ontario on 1 January 2022 is brought into the electronic monitoring regime and remains subject to the maintenance duty that attached on that date. The duty does not evaporate because headcount subsequently falls below 25.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That crystallises the s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation and the s.74.1 disconnecting from work obligation on the transitional basis. Headcount fell to 24 after the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 and stayed at 24 through 2 January 2023, but the statutory trigger is the 1 January 2022 snapshot.

On the facts D has a written and appropriately distributed disconnecting from work policy, so that limb is satisfied. D has “not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. A written electronic monitoring policy was required for a 25+ employer on 1 January 2022 by 1 July 2022 and is still absent on 2 January 2023. That is a complete absence of a statutorily required written policy for an employer captured on the qualifying date.

A is 20 on 2 January 2023, the 8 agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023, so <25 on the date in issue.
B is 23 on the date in issue, <25 on 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022. The voluntarily adopted policies do not create a statutory distribution duty where the 25 employee threshold is not met.
E is 18 on 2 January 2023 after August resignations and 31 December retirements, the 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue.

C is a ~1,000 employee employer throughout 2022 and the fact pattern states it has a written electronic monitoring policy and a written disconnecting from work policy and that both have been written and appropriately distributed. The monthly review / quarterly hand-out described is a business implementation of distribution for a large workforce. 3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in play on 2 Jan 2023 are s.74.2 electronic monitoring and s.74.1 disconnecting from work for employers who regularly employ 25+ in Ontario. Electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 25+ class, disconnect in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class. Policy must be given within 30 days of hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change.

The Working for Workers Two 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 with a compliance window to 2 June 2023. On 2 Jan 2023 the immediate statutory duties remain 25+, so A, B and E are below threshold on the date in issue and no 10+ duty is immediately enforceable.

* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25, no s.74.1/74.2 duty.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021. Majority view: no statutory policy duty; voluntary adoption does not create a statutory distribution obligation, refusal to distribute to new hires is not an ESA breach where threshold not met.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on qualifying dates and date in issue, no duty.

The disagreement is D vs C.

D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, has not developed an electronic monitoring policy.

Lock-in/snapshot camp: coverage crystallises on 1 Jan 2022 for the first Working for Workers Act cohort. An employer 25+ on that snapshot is brought within s.74.2 and the 25+ disconnect regime and the duty is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall to 24. D therefore remains obliged to maintain a written electronic monitoring policy; its complete absence on 2 Jan 2023 is a categorical s.74.2 breach. Disconnect limb is satisfied.

Ongoing regularly-employs camp: duty is assessed by current regular employment on 2 Jan 2023. D regularly employs 24 <25, so no present s.74.1/74.2 duty; the disconnect policy is permissive and the lack of an electronic monitoring policy is not presently a breach.

C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies.

30-day update dispute: C amends both policies every month but provides a copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter. Strict reading: a monthly amendment triggers a 30-day update duty; quarterly hand-out can be up to ~90 days after change, breach of ss.74.1 and 74.2 maintenance/distribution. Counter reading: fact pattern states policies are written and appropriately distributed; monthly “updates” may be internal/admin/housekeeping not material changes requiring re-issue; quarterly dissemination is reasonable for a ~1,000 person employer and does not establish a demonstrable 30-day violation.

Current split in round 2: a significant minority holds C is the clear 30-day update/distribution breach under an ongoing regularly-employs reading where D is no longer 25+. The majority in the room still treats the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot as lock-in for the first cohort and identifies D’s complete absence of a required electronic monitoring policy triggered by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 as the cleanest, binary non-compliance.

Unresolved pivotal points remain:
* Lock-in vs ongoing regularly employs test for D’s electronic monitoring duty after fall to 24.
* Whether C’s monthly update/quarterly hand-out is a statutory 30-day breach or a permissible business practice consistent with “appropriately distributed”.
* The precise evidentiary weight of the statement that C’s policies are “appropriately distributed” versus an inferred timing defect.

I remain with D as the prevailing best answer under the conventional 1 Jan 2022 snapshot/lock-in reading, while recognising the credible C update-timing argument that is being advanced under an ongoing headcount reading.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains split on two interpretive drivers that decide the answer: 
(1) whether the 25-employee test for the Working for Workers Act, 2021 policies is a one-time lock-in on the 1 Jan 2022 / 1 July 2022 snapshot or an ongoing “regularly employs 25 or more” current head-count test; and 
(2) whether the 10+ disconnecting-from-work expansion is already immediately compliant on 2 Jan 2023 or is phased with compliance to 2 June 2023.

Common facts now accepted:
* s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring: 25+ employer duty, in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort, written policy required, give on hire within 30 days and updated copy within 30 days of a change.
* s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work: 25+ employer duty, in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class, same distribution/update duties.
* 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 but the 10-24 compliance window runs to 2 June 2023 in the prevailing reading used by the majority in round 2. A minority reads the 10+ duty as immediate on 2 Jan 2023.

Options on 2 Jan 2023 under the prevailing 25+ lock-in + phased 10+ reading:

A. 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the material date and on the qualifying dates. No s.74.1/s.74.2 duty. Under an immediate 10+ reading A would need a disconnect policy and would be non-compliant.

B. 23 employees. <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. No statutory 25+ duty. Employer has voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021 and refuses to distribute to new hires on cost grounds. Majority view: refusal is not a statutory breach because threshold not met. Minority 10+ immediate view: 23 triggers a disconnect duty and refusal to distribute breaches s.74.1 disclosure.

C. ~1,000 employees throughout 2022, 987-1,012 range, >>25. Has written and “appropriately distributed” both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Updates policies every month but provides a copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter.
The 30-day update/distribution controversy: monthly amendment + quarterly hand-out can leave employees >30 days, up to ~90 days, on a superseded version. Colleagues 1,15,16,18 argue this is a breach of the 30-day update rule for both policies. Colleagues 2,5,8,9,14 argue “appropriately distributed” and that monthly edits are not established as material changes requiring re-issue; quarterly dissemination is a reasonable implementation and not proven non-compliant on these facts.

D. 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 24 after 6 terminations on 15 Mar 2022, no further change. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy ever developed.
Lock-in view: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 crystallises s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation by 1 July 2022 and the duty is not retroactively extinguished by the fall to 24. Absence of an electronic monitoring policy on 2 Jan 2023 is a categorical breach. Ongoing head-count view: on 2 Jan 2023 employer regularly employs 24 <25, so no current s.74.1/s.74.2 duty; the disconnect policy is superfluous but not a breach. This is the main split.

E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires not effective until 15 Feb 2023 → 24. On 2 Jan 2023 18 <25, no statutory duty under 25+ test. Under an immediate 10+ disconnect expansion E would need a disconnect policy and would be non-compliant.

Errors / corrections noted across rounds:
* Colleague 4’s claim that electronic monitoring duty is not size-based is inconsistent with s.74.2.
* The electronic monitoring in-force date is often cited as 1 Jan 2022 with compliance by 1 July 2022; disconnect 25+ is 2 June/1 July 2022.

Unresolved / carried forward:
* Exact effective/compliance date for 10+ disconnect: immediate 1 Jan 2023 vs compliance by 2 June 2023. This changes A, B, E.
* Whether 25-employee test is lock-in on 1 Jan 2022 or ongoing regularly employs. This determines D’s liability and whether a later dip below 25 extinguishes duty.
* Precise 30-day update rule for C: does monthly “update” equal a policy change requiring distribution within 30 days, and does the stated “appropriately distributed” defeat the breach finding?

Current best synthesis given the prevailing exam reading in the room: D is the clearest statutory breach under the 25+ lock-in reading – an employer 30 on 1 Jan 2022 remains obliged to maintain a written electronic monitoring policy, which it has never developed, whereas A, B and E are below 25 on the material date and C’s breach hinges on the contested update-distribution timing interpretation. A substantial minority now votes C on the 30-day update argument; a minority votes B under an immediate 10+ reading.

reflection_text.3:
The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in play on 2 Jan 2023 are s.74.2 electronic monitoring and s.74.1 disconnecting from work for employers who regularly employ 25+ in Ontario. Electronic monitoring in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 25+ class, disconnect in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class. Policy must be given within 30 days of hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change.

The Working for Workers Two 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 with a compliance window to 2 June 2023. On 2 Jan 2023 the immediate statutory duties remain 25+, so A, B and E are below threshold on the date in issue and no 10+ duty is immediately enforceable.

* A: 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25, no s.74.1/74.2 duty.
* B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Voluntary disconnect policy since 2020 and online monitoring policy since late 2021. Majority view: no statutory policy duty; voluntary adoption does not create a statutory distribution obligation, refusal to distribute to new hires is not an ESA breach where threshold not met.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023. <25 on qualifying dates and date in issue, no duty.

The disagreement is D vs C.

D: 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 employees thereafter. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, has not developed an electronic monitoring policy.

Lock-in/snapshot camp: coverage crystallises on 1 Jan 2022 for the first Working for Workers Act cohort. An employer 25+ on that snapshot is brought within s.74.2 and the 25+ disconnect regime and the duty is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall to 24. D therefore remains obliged to maintain a written electronic monitoring policy; its complete absence on 2 Jan 2023 is a categorical s.74.2 breach. Disconnect limb is satisfied.

Ongoing regularly-employs camp: duty is assessed by current regular employment on 2 Jan 2023. D regularly employs 24 <25, so no present s.74.1/74.2 duty; the disconnect policy is permissive and the lack of an electronic monitoring policy is not presently a breach.

C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies.

30-day update dispute: C amends both policies every month but provides a copy to each employee only every fiscal quarter. Strict reading: a monthly amendment triggers a 30-day update duty; quarterly hand-out can be up to ~90 days after change, breach of ss.74.1 and 74.2 maintenance/distribution. Counter reading: fact pattern states policies are written and appropriately distributed; monthly “updates” may be internal/admin/housekeeping not material changes requiring re-issue; quarterly dissemination is reasonable for a ~1,000 person employer and does not establish a demonstrable 30-day violation.

Current split in round 2: a significant minority holds C is the clear 30-day update/distribution breach under an ongoing regularly-employs reading where D is no longer 25+. The majority in the room still treats the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot as lock-in for the first cohort and identifies D’s complete absence of a required electronic monitoring policy triggered by 30 employees on 1 Jan 2022 as the cleanest, binary non-compliance.

Unresolved pivotal points remain:
* Lock-in vs ongoing regularly employs test for D’s electronic monitoring duty after fall to 24.
* Whether C’s monthly update/quarterly hand-out is a statutory 30-day breach or a permissible business practice consistent with “appropriately distributed”.
* The precise evidentiary weight of the statement that C’s policies are “appropriately distributed” versus an inferred timing defect.

I remain with D as the prevailing best answer under the conventional 1 Jan 2022 snapshot/lock-in reading, while recognising the credible C update-timing argument that is being advanced under an ongoing headcount reading.

* s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work – written policy for employers who regularly employ 25+ employees, in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort, same give-on-hire and 30-day update duties.
* The 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 but the compliance window for the 10-24 cohort runs to 2 June 2023, so the immediate mandatory duties on 2 Jan 2023 remain 25+.

D was 30 on 1 Jan 2022, so s.74.2 electronic monitoring attached by 1 July 2022 and remains unmet on 2 Jan 2023. The unambiguous breach then shifts to C: >25 employer with written policies but updates both policies every month and only hands an updated copy to employees once per fiscal quarter, which can be >30 days, up to ~90 days, after a change, breaching the 30-day update/distribution requirement under ss.74.1 and 74.2. This is the position of Colleagues 1, 15, 16, 18, 4, 3.

B distribution issue is marginal now. Voluntary adoption below the 25-employee threshold does not create a statutory distribution duty for the 25+ regimes; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach where the threshold is not met. The size-neutral electronic monitoring claim is rejected by the majority.

The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in play on 2 Jan 2023 are s.74.2 electronic monitoring and s.74.1 disconnecting from work, both for an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario. 
* s.74.2: written policy, give on hire within 30 days and updated copy within 30 days of a change; in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 25+ class, compliance for the first cohort by 1 July 2022.
* s.74.1: written policy, give on hire within 30 days and updated copy within 30 days of a change; in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.
The 10+ disconnect expansion made by Working for Workers Act, 2022 is in force 1 Jan 2023 but the implementation window for the 10-24 cohort runs to 2 June 2023, so on 2 Jan 2023 the immediate statutory policy duties remain 25+ duties.

Headcounts on 2 Jan 2023 and on qualifying dates
* A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022, 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023. <25 on all relevant dates.
* B: 23 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has voluntary disconnect 2020 and online monitoring 2021; refuses distribution to new hires on cost.
* D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → 24 after 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022, no further change. 24 on 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy; no electronic monitoring policy.
* E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 18 on 2 Jan 2023; 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. <25 on all relevant dates.
* C: c.1,000 on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. >>25. Has written and appropriately distributed both disconnecting-from-work and electronic monitoring policies. Updates both policies every month; provides a copy of the updated policies to each employee every fiscal quarter.

Core disagreement retained from prior round and reinforced in round 2

Snapshot / lock-in reading for D. The 1 Jan 2022 headcount is the transitional qualifying date for the first compliance cohort. An employer who was 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 is brought within s.74.2 and the 25+ disconnect class and the duty that crystallises on that snapshot is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall below 25. Under that reading D is still covered on 2 Jan 2023 despite being 24. D has a disconnect policy but “has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all, a categorical breach of s.74.2. This is the majority position in round 2: Colleagues 10,11,12,13,14,17,2,5,6,7,8,9.

Ongoing “regularly employs 25+” reading. The test is continuing and assessed on the date in issue. On 2 Jan 2023 A, B, D and E are <25, so the 25+ statutory policy duties are not engaged for them. D’s disconnect policy is voluntary; absence of an electronic monitoring policy is not required at current headcount. Under this reading the only 25+ employer is C. The breach then becomes C’s maintenance/distribution timing: s.74.1 and s.74.2 require an updated copy within 30 days of a change. C amends both policies every month but only hands out a copy quarterly, so employees can receive a policy up to ~90 days after a change. Colleagues 1,15,16,18,4 argue this is a 30-day update/distribution breach; Colleagues 13,14,8 argue the monthly “updates” are not proven to be material changes requiring re-issue and the fact pattern expressly says policies are “appropriately distributed”.

Unresolved / contested points still live
* Whether “regularly employs 25 or more” is a one-time transitional snapshot on 1 Jan 2022 for electronic monitoring and 1 July 2022 for disconnect, with coverage locked in despite a later fall below 25, or a continuing test assessed on 2 Jan 2023. D is the test case.
* Whether C’s monthly amendment/quarterly hand-out practice violates the 30-day update rule. Dispute is over whether each monthly edit is a statutory “change to the policy” and over how to read “appropriately distributed”.
* 10+ disconnect expansion. Minority raised 10+ disconnect effective 1 Jan 2023. Majority treatment keeps the immediate duty at 25+ with a compliance window to 2 June 2023 for 10-24; if the 10+ duty were immediate, A and E would also lack a required disconnect policy and B’s refusal to distribute would become a statutory distribution breach, making the question under-determined.
* Errors noted and now largely settled: electronic monitoring is size-based 25+, not a universal disclosure duty; refusal to distribute a voluntarily adopted policy for an under-threshold employer is not a statutory ESA breach.

Current synthesis: under the snapshot lock-in reading the statutory gap is unambiguous for D: a 30-employee employer on 1 Jan 2022 remains obliged to have a written electronic monitoring policy on 2 Jan 2023 and has none. Under the ongoing regularly-employs reading the only 25+ employer on 2 Jan 2023 is C and its monthly-update/quarterly-distribution practice is the plausible 30-day update/distribution breach. The central tension remains the snapshot vs ongoing interpretation of the 25-employee test and the materiality of C’s monthly updates.

* s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring – a written policy; give on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change. In force 1 January 2022 for the 25+ class, compliance 1 July 2022.
* s.74.1 ESA right to disconnect – a written policy; give on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change. In force 2 June / 1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.

The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ right-to-disconnect expansion is in force 1 January 2023 but the 10-24 implementation window runs to 2 June 2023, so on 2 January 2023 the statutory duties remain 25+ duties.

Threshold on the operative dates

* A 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023. <25 on the 1 January 2022 trigger date and on the date in issue. No s.74.1 / s.74.2 duty attaches on 2 January 2023.
* B 23 employees on 2 January 2023, <25 on 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022. Neither the electronic monitoring nor the statutory disconnect duty is engaged. The disconnect policy in place since 2020 and the online monitoring policy in place since late 2021 are voluntary; voluntary adoption does not create a statutory distribution obligation where the 25 employee threshold is not met.
* E 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. 18 employees on 2 January 2023 <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue. No statutory policy duty arises as of 2 January 2023.
* C c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. Unambiguously 25+ on the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger. The fact pattern states the employer has a written electronic monitoring policy and a written disconnecting-from-work policy and that both are written and appropriately distributed. That is the policy in place required by ss.74.1 and 74.2 on the date in issue.

D employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That 25+ headcount on the transitional qualifying date crystallises the s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation and the 25+ s.74.1 disconnecting-from-work obligation for the initial Working for Workers Act, 2021 cohort. The duty that attaches on the 1 January 2022 snapshot is not retroactively extinguished by the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 that reduce headcount to 24 thereafter.

On the facts D “has written and appropriately distributed a policy on disconnecting from work” so that limb is satisfied for the 25+ cohort. D “has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. A written electronic monitoring policy was required by 1 July 2022 for an employer who was 25+ on 1 January 2022 and the absence is still unremedied on 2 January 2023.

That is a categorical failure to have the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy in place and available to the workforce for a 25+ employer captured on the 1 January 2022 transitional date. A, B and E are below the 25 employee mandatory threshold on 2 January 2023 and C is described as having the required written policies in place and appropriately distributed.

The clear statutory non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 is D.
public_text.3:
On 2 January 2023 the only mandatory written-policy duties that are immediately enforceable are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ duties.

* ESA s.74.2 electronic monitoring – an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario shall have a written electronic monitoring policy, give a copy to an employee within 30 days of hire and give an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. In force 1 January 2022 for the 25+ class.
* ESA s.74.1 right to disconnect – an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario shall have a written disconnecting-from-work policy, give a copy within 30 days of hire and give an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. In force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.

The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 January 2023 but the implementation window for the 10-24 cohort runs to 2 June 2023. On 2 January 2023 the statutory policy duties are therefore still 25+ duties and “regularly employs 25 or more” is a continuing size test assessed on the date in issue.

* A – 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023. <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue. No s.74.1/s.74.2 duty attaches on 2 January 2023.
* B – 23 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022. Neither the electronic monitoring nor the statutory disconnect duty is engaged. The disconnecting-from-work and online monitoring policies in place since 2020/2021 are voluntary; where the 25 employee threshold is not met the ESA does not impose a statutory distribution obligation in respect of a voluntarily adopted policy.
* E – 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. 18 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue. No s.74.1/s.74.2 duty arises as of 2 January 2023.

D – 30 employees on 1 January 2022, 24 employees after the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 and unchanged thereafter. On a continuing regularly-employs reading D regularly employs 24 employees on 2 January 2023, i.e. <25. It is therefore not presently obliged to maintain a statutory s.74.2 electronic monitoring policy and is not presently obliged to maintain a statutory s.74.1 disconnecting-from-work policy. The written and appropriately distributed disconnecting-from-work policy it holds is permissive. On the ongoing test the absence of an electronic monitoring policy is not a current statutory breach.

C is unequivocally in the 25+ class. c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022 and 987-1,012 at all times in 2022, so both the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger are met. A written electronic monitoring policy and a written disconnecting-from-work policy are in place and were initially distributed.

The continuing duty is maintenance/distribution. Ss.74.1 and 74.2 require an updated copy of a required policy to be provided to each employee within 30 days of a change to the policy. C amends both the disconnecting-from-work policy and the electronic monitoring policy every month but only hands an updated copy to the workforce once per fiscal quarter. A monthly amendment followed by a quarterly hand-out can leave employees working for up to ~90 days under a superseded version of a required policy. That is provision of an updated policy more than 30 days after the change and is a failure of the 30-day update/distribution obligation under both s.74.1 and s.74.2 for both the disconnecting-from-work and the electronic monitoring regimes on 2 January 2023.

That timely-update/distribution failure is the statutory non-compliance present on 2 January 2023. On an ongoing regularly-employs reading D is not presently in breach and C is the clear breach.

On 2 January 2023 the immediately operative written-policy duties are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 duties for the 25+ class.

* s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring – an employer who regularly employs 25 or more employees in Ontario must have a written electronic monitoring policy, give a copy to each employee within 30 days of hire and give an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy. In force 1 January 2022 for the 1 January 2022 25+ cohort, compliance by 1 July 2022.
* s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work – same form of duty. In force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort.

The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ right-to-disconnect expansion is in force 1 January 2023 but the implementation window for the 10-24 cohort runs to 2 June 2023. On 2 January 2023 the statutory policy duties remain 25+ duties.

Headcount on the operative dates

A. 20 employees on 1 January 2022 and 20 employees on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023. <25 on the 1 January 2022 qualifying date and on the date in issue. No s.74.1/ s.74.2 duty attaches on 2 January 2023.

B. 23 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022. Neither the electronic monitoring nor the statutory disconnect duty is engaged. The disconnect and online monitoring policies in place since 2020/2021 are voluntary. Voluntary adoption does not create a statutory distribution obligation where the 25 employee threshold is not met; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a s.74.1/74.2 breach on a <25 headcount.

E. 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. 18 employees on 2 January 2023. <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue. No statutory policy duty arises as of 2 January 2023.

C. c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. The employer is unequivocally 25+ on both the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger and is therefore subject to both regimes. The fact pattern states the employer has written and appropriately distributed both a disconnecting-from-work policy and an electronic monitoring policy. That is the required policy suite for a 25+ employer on 2 January 2023.

D. 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That 25+ headcount on the transitional qualifying date crystallises the s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation with compliance by 1 July 2022 and the s.74.1 disconnecting-from-work obligation for the 25+ cohort. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reduce headcount to 24 thereafter and headcount stays at 24 through 2 January 2023, but the transitional coverage for the first Working for Workers Act, 2021 cohort is fixed by the 1 January 2022 snapshot and is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall below 25.

On the facts D “has written and appropriately distributed a policy on disconnecting from work and has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. The disconnect limb is satisfied. The electronic monitoring policy required by s.74.2 ESA for a 25+ employer on the 1 January 2022 snapshot is still completely absent on 2 January 2023.

That is a categorical failure to have the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy in place and available to the workforce. A and B and E are below the 25+ threshold on the material dates and C has the required written policies in place and distributed on the facts as stated.

The clear, undisputed statutory non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 is D.

**D**

As of 2 January 2023 the mandatory written-policy duties that are in force are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ duties

* ESA s.74.2 electronic monitoring – written policy, copy on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy, in force 1 Jan 2022 for the 25+ class, with the first compliance date 1 July 2022; and
* ESA s.74.1 right to disconnect – written policy, copy on hire and an updated copy within 30 days of a change to the policy, in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.

For the first compliance cohort the 25+ class is fixed by the 1 January 2022 headcount. An employer who regularly employed 25 or more employees in Ontario on 1 January 2022 is brought within s.74.2 and the 25+ disconnect class and the duty that crystallises on that snapshot is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall in headcount during the 2022 transition year.

* A. 20 employees on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 employees on 2 Jan 2023. The 8 agreements do not commence until 10 Jan 2023. <25 on the qualifying date and on the date in issue, no s.74.1/74.2 duty attaches on 2 Jan 2023.

* B. 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Neither the electronic monitoring nor the statutory disconnect duty is engaged. The disconnect and online monitoring policies adopted in 2020/2021 are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntarily adopted policy is not an ESA breach where the 25 employee threshold is not met.

* E. 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after the August 2022 resignations → 18 after the 31 Dec 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 Feb 2023. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023 <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue, no statutory policy duty arises.

* C. c.1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. The employer is unambiguously a 25+ employer on both the 1 Jan 2022 electronic monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger. The fact pattern states the employer “has written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring”. It is a covered 25+ employer with the required written policies in place and distributed on the date in issue.

* D. Employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That 25+ headcount on the operative qualifying date crystallises the s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation and the 25+ s.74.1 disconnecting-from-work obligation for the initial Working for Workers Act, 2021 cohort. The six terminations on 15 March 2022 reducing headcount to 24, and the fact headcount remains 24 through 2 January 2023, do not unwind the duty that attached on the 1 January 2022 snapshot.

On the facts D “has written and appropriately distributed a policy on disconnecting from work” so that limb for the 25+ cohort is satisfied, but D “has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. An electronic monitoring policy was required by 1 July 2022 for a 25+ employer on the 1 January 2022 snapshot and is still completely absent on 2 January 2023.

The categorical non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 is therefore D’s missing electronic monitoring policy.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments in play on 2 Jan 2023 are the 25+ employee duties:

* s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring – written policy for employer who regularly employed 25+ in Ontario on 1 Jan 2022, in force 1 Jan 2022, compliance by 1 Jul 2022; copy on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change.
* s.74.1 ESA disconnecting from work – written policy for employer who regularly employs 25+ in Ontario, in force 2 Jun/1 Jul 2022 for the 25+ cohort; same give-on-hire and 30-day update duties.

The 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 but the compliance window for the 10-24 cohort runs to 2 Jun 2023, so the immediate statutory policy duties on 2 Jan 2023 remain 25+ duties.

Headcount snapshots:

A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023. 8 hires effective 10 Jan 2023. <25 on date in issue → no statutory duty.

B: 23 employees on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 Jul 2022. No statutory 25+ duty. Voluntary disconnect and online monitoring policies since 2020/2021; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach where threshold not met.

E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements. 6 hires effective 15 Feb 2023. 18 employees on 2 Jan 2023 <25 on all relevant dates → no statutory duty.

C: ~1,000 employees on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022. Clearly 25+ on both trigger dates. Fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Dispute is maintenance/distribution: policies updated every month but copy provided every fiscal quarter. Current round majority treat the explicit “appropriately distributed” statement as sufficient and/or read monthly updates as not established as material changes requiring re-issue within 30 days; the 30-day update argument is characterised as interpretive/timing debate not a categorical breach.

D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022, 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter, no further change. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy; has no electronic monitoring policy at all.

Central divide remains lock-in vs current headcount:

Lock-in view: 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 crystallises electronic monitoring duty for the initial Working for Workers cohort and is not retroactively extinguished by a later fall below 25. On that view D is in breach for lacking electronic monitoring policy required by 1 Jan 2022 and still missing on 2 Jan 2023; disconnect policy is present so that limb is satisfied. This is the position of Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,16,18,2,4,5,6,7,8,9.

Current-headcount view: duty is ongoing “regularly employs 25 or more” on 2 Jan 2023. D regularly employs 24 on 2 Jan 2023 so no statutory electronic monitoring duty presently; defect then shifts to C’s update timing. Colleagues 17 and 3 adopt this reading and identify C’s monthly update/quarterly hand-out as a breach of the 30-day update rule.

Round 3 distribution: D is overwhelming majority ~16 colleagues; C is minority ~2 colleagues. The lock-in reading for D remains the most consistently supported statutory breach. C’s update/distribution timing remains the main competing theory under a current-headcount reading.

Unresolved tensions carried forward:
* Whether the 1 Jan 2022 25-employee snapshot permanently locks in electronic monitoring/disconnect duties or duty is assessed by current “regularly employs” headcount on 2 Jan 2023.
* Whether C’s monthly update/quarterly hand-out is a per se breach of the 30-day update-distribution requirement or is covered by the fact pattern’s statement that policies are “appropriately distributed” and that updates may not be material changes.
* Minority 10+ disconnect expansion argument that would make A, B and E non-compliant is not pursued in current round.

I retain D’s missing electronic monitoring policy triggered by 30-employee 1 Jan 2022 count as the most consistently supported statutory breach on a lock-in 25+ reading, with C’s update/distribution timing as the main competing theory under a current-headcount reading.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Working for Workers Act, 2021 ESA amendments are the operative frame on 2 Jan 2023.

* s.74.2 electronic monitoring – 25+ employees, written policy, give on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change. In force 1 Jan 2022 for the 1 Jan 2022 cohort, compliance by 1 July 2022.
* s.74.1 disconnecting from work – 25+ employees, same form of duty. In force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort.
The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ right-to-disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 with an implementation window to 2 June 2023, so on 2 Jan 2023 the immediately enforceable mandatory duties remain 25+.

Head-counts on the dates that matter:
A: 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → <25 on both qualifying date and date in issue.
B: 23 on 2 Jan 2023; <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Disconnect and online monitoring policies since 2020/2021 are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory breach where 25+ not met.
C: ~1,000 on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → unambiguously 25+ on both triggers. Fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed disconnect and electronic monitoring policies. Monthly internal “updates” with quarterly hand-outs is the contested maintenance point.
D: 30 on 1 Jan 2022 → 24 after 6 terminations 15 Mar 2022, stays 24. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, no electronic monitoring policy at all.
E: 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements; 6 hires not effective until 15 Feb 2023 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023.

Round 3 public positions:
Majority D camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,16,18,2,4,5,6,7,8,9. Argument: the first 2021 cohort is fixed by the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot. D was 30 on 1 Jan 2022, so s.74.2 electronic monitoring attached with compliance by 1 July 2022 and is not retroactively extinguished by the fall to 24. D has a disconnect policy but no electronic monitoring policy at all → categorical breach. A,B,E are <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and therefore have no mandatory s.74.1/s.74.2 duty; B’s refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not a statutory breach under 25+. C is described as having written and appropriately distributed policies; monthly review/quarterly issuance is a business implementation debate, not a proven material change left undistributed >30 days.

Minority C camp – Colleagues 17 and 3 in this round. Argument: “regularly employs” is an ongoing test on 2 Jan 2023. D now regularly employs 24, so not currently in the 25+ class; its disconnect policy is permissive. C is unequivocally 25+ and has policies, but monthly amendment with quarterly hand-out means employees can receive an update up to ~90 days after a change, breaching the 30-day update/distribution requirement under ss.74.1/74.2.

Unresolved tensions carried forward:
* Lock-in vs continuing regularly employs reading for the 25+ first cohort. Snapshot camp says 1 Jan 2022 coverage is fixed for the transition year and prevents evasion; continuing camp says duty follows current headcount.
* Whether C’s monthly “updates” are material changes to the policy triggering the 30-day re-issue duty, and whether quarterly distribution to ~1,000 employees is per se non-compliant or a reasonable implementation of “appropriately distributed”.
* Interaction of the 10+ disconnect expansion compliance window to 2 June 2023 with the 2 Jan 2023 assessment date; no colleague now sustains a B breach on that basis.

Current best synthesis: Conventional teaching and the majority of colleagues emphasise the 1 Jan 2022 lock-in for the first compliance cohort, making D the definitive non-compliance for the complete absence of the statutorily required electronic monitoring policy that attached on 1 Jan 2022. C’s 30-day update argument is plausible under a strict continuing test and literal reading, but it requires inferring a material change each month and treating quarterly distribution as non-compliant, whereas D’s breach is a clear missing required policy. A, B, E remain below the 25+ threshold on 2 Jan 2023 and therefore have no mandatory s.74.1/s.74.2 duty on that date.

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The immediate mandatory written-policy duties on 2 Jan 2023 are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ duties. s.74.2 ESA electronic monitoring – written policy, copy on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change – in force 1 Jan 2022 for the first cohort, compliance 1 July 2022. s.74.1 ESA right to disconnect – written policy, copy on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change – in force 2 June/1 July 2022 for the 25+ cohort. The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 Jan 2023 but the 10-24 implementation window runs to 2 June 2023, so the statutory duties immediately enforceable on 2 Jan 2023 remain 25+.

Headcounts on the material dates:
* A – 20 on 1 Jan 2022 and 20 on 2 Jan 2023; 8 hires start 10 Jan 2023 → <25 on qualifying date and date in issue.
* B – 23 on 2 Jan 2023, <25 on 1 Jan 2022 and 1 July 2022. Has voluntary disconnect since 2020 and online monitoring since late 2021 but refuses distribution to new hires.
* E – 22 on 1 Jan 2022 → 20 after Aug 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 Dec 2022 retirements; 6 hires not effective until 15 Feb 2023 → 18 on 2 Jan 2023 <25.
* C – c.1,000 on 1 Jan 2022, 987-1,012 throughout 2022 → unequivocally 25+ on both triggers. Fact pattern states written and appropriately distributed both disconnect and electronic-monitoring policies; updates policies every month and provides a copy to each employee every fiscal quarter.
* D – 30 on 1 Jan 2022, –6 terminations 15 Mar 2022 → 24 thereafter through 2 Jan 2023. Has written and appropriately distributed disconnect policy, has never developed an electronic-monitoring policy.

Competing readings:
Lock-in/snapshot for the 2021 cohort vs ongoing regularly employs. Majority in rounds 2-3 adopt the 1 Jan 2022 snapshot/lock-in for the first Working for Workers Act, 2021 cohort: an employer 25+ on 1 Jan 2022 remains in scope for the transition year even if headcount later falls below 25. On that reading D’s s.74.2 electronic-monitoring duty crystallised on 1 Jan 2022 with compliance by 1 July 2022 and is still unmet on 2 Jan 2023. D’s disconnect policy is present, so only electronic monitoring is missing.

Current-head-count/regularly employs reading would make D <25 on 2 Jan 2023 and not presently required to maintain an electronic-monitoring policy, moving the breach to C. Colleague 17 and others on that reading point to C’s monthly amendment/quarterly hand-out as a >30-day lag for updated policies for both disconnect and electronic monitoring, so C would be non-compliant on update-distribution timing.

B distribution refusal: majority view is <25 means no statutory policy duty is engaged; voluntary adoption does not create statutory distribution obligation, so refusal is not an ESA breach. Minority in round 0 treated B as breach.

C update issue: minority argue monthly policy amendments with quarterly dissemination is textbook >30-day lag, breach of s.74.1/74.2 update duty. On 2 January 2023 the written-policy duties that are immediately enforceable are the Working for Workers Act, 2021 25+ duties.

* ESA s.74.2 electronic monitoring: written policy, copy on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change. In force 1 January 2022 for employers who regularly employed 25+ in Ontario on 1 January 2022, compliance 1 July 2022.
* ESA s.74.1 right to disconnect: written policy, copy on hire and updated copy within 30 days of a change. In force 2 June / 1 July 2022 for the 25+ class.

The Working for Workers Act, 2022 10+ disconnect expansion is in force 1 January 2023 but the 10-24 implementation window runs to 2 June 2023. On 2 January 2023 the immediately operative statutory duties remain the 25+ duties.

Headcount / coverage on the operative dates

A. 20 on 1 January 2022 and 20 on 2 January 2023. The 8 agreements do not commence until 10 January 2023. <25 on the qualifying date and on the date in issue. No s.74.1 / s.74.2 duty.

B. 23 employees on 2 January 2023, <25 on 1 January 2022 and 1 July 2022. Neither the electronic monitoring nor the statutory disconnect duty is engaged. The disconnect and online monitoring policies adopted in 2020/2021 are voluntary; refusal to distribute a voluntary policy is not an ESA breach where the 25 employee threshold is not met.

E. 22 on 1 January 2022 → 20 after August 2022 resignations → 18 after 31 December 2022 retirements. The 6 hires are not effective until 15 February 2023. 18 employees on 2 January 2023 <25 on the qualifying dates and on the date in issue. No statutory policy duty arises.

C. c.1,000 employees on 1 January 2022, 987-1,012 at all times in 2022. Unambiguously 25+ on both the 1 January 2022 electronic monitoring trigger and the 1 July 2022 disconnect trigger. The fact pattern expressly states the employer “has written and appropriately distributed both a policy on disconnecting from work and a policy on electronic monitoring”. That is the required written-policy suite for a 25+ employer on 2 January 2023. The monthly review / quarterly hand-out point is a process debate about what constitutes a material change triggering the 30-day update duty; the facts expressly characterise distribution as appropriate.

D. Employed 30 individuals on 1 January 2022. That 25+ headcount on the transitional qualifying date crystallises the s.74.2 electronic monitoring obligation with compliance by 1 July 2022 and the s.74.1 25+ disconnect obligation for the first Working for Workers Act, 2021 cohort. The duty that attaches on the 1 January 2022 snapshot is not retroactively extinguished by the 6 terminations on 15 March 2022 that reduce headcount to 24 thereafter and keep it at 24 through 2 January 2023.

On the facts D “has written and appropriately distributed a policy on disconnecting from work and has not developed a policy on electronic monitoring” at all. The disconnect limb is satisfied. The electronic monitoring policy required by s.74.2 for a 25+ employer on 1 January 2022 is completely absent on 2 January 2023.

That is a categorical failure to have the statutorily required written electronic monitoring policy in place and available to the workforce for an employer captured on the 1 January 2022 snapshot. A, B and E are below the 25 employee threshold on the material dates and C is described as having the required written and appropriately distributed policies.

The clear statutory non-compliance as of 2 January 2023 is D.
